summary: Explains how to build and read PKIX certificates used for SIP over TLS, in particular how to encode a SIP domain identity in a certificate and use it to authenticate a SIP domain. It is aimed at SIP implementers and certificate issuers. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a SIP client connects to a server over TLS, the server shows a certificate and the client checks it. This RFC says what a SIP domain name looks like inside that certificate, where it must go, and how two domain names must be compared so that the check cannot be fooled.

questions: how to authenticate a sip domain
where does a sip certificate store the domain name
how does a sip client verify a tls server
subtitle: How a SIP server proves it is authoritative for a domain, using an X.509 certificate.

tldr.problem: SIP over TLS needs certificates, but the SIP specification never said where to put a domain name in a certificate or which name to trust when a certificate holds several.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC puts the SIP domain identity in the subjectAltName extension as a uniformResourceIdentifier, defines how to extract identities from a certificate, and defines how to compare them against the domain the caller asked for.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from June 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3261 and forbids wildcard and suffix matching, so a certificate for one domain does not cover another.

facts.label: Recommended place for a SIP identity
Backward-compatible fallback
facts.value: The CN field of the Subject, only when subjectAltName is absent

facts.label: Accepted identity types
facts.value: URI and DNS in the subjectAltName field

facts.label: Certificate validation
facts.value: Follow the procedures of RFC 5280 and check extendedKeyUsage

today: RFC 5922 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2010 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3261, whose Section 26.3.1 previously said only that a SIP server should hold a site certificate matching its canonical host name, and the editorial appendix in this RFC proposes the replacement wording for the next comprehensive update of that document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Transport Layer Security, specified in RFC 5246, is available in an increasing number of Session Initiation Protocol implementations. RFC 3261 defines SIP. To use the authentication capabilities of TLS, certificates as defined by the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure in RFC 5280 are required.

Existing SIP specifications do not sufficiently specify how to use certificates for domain authentication, as opposed to host authentication. This document gives guidance to ensure interoperability and uniform conventions for the construction and interpretation of certificates used to identify their holders as authoritative for a domain.

The discussion is confined to an X.509 PKIX-compliant certificate used for a TLS connection. The document does not define the use of such certificates for any other purpose, such as Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions.

One definition is added. A SIP domain identity is an identity, for example sip:example.com, contained in an X.509 certificate bound to a subject that identifies the subject as an authoritative SIP server for a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP server that wants to be trusted over an encrypted connection needs an X.509 certificate. This RFC says what to put in that certificate when the thing being claimed is authority over a whole SIP domain.

sections.title: Why Certificates Were Ambiguous
sections.content:
TLS uses the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure of RFC 5280 to bind an identity, or a set of identities, to the subject of an X.509 certificate. RFC 3261 gives adequate guidance on the use of X.509 certificates for S/MIME but is relatively silent on their use for TLS.

The security properties of TLS and S/MIME as used in SIP are different. X.509 certificates for S/MIME are generally used for end-to-end authentication and encryption, so they serve to bind the identity of a user to the certificate, and RFC 3261 is clear that in such certificates the subjectAltName field holds the appropriate identity. X.509 certificates used for TLS serve instead to bind the identities of the per-hop domain sending or receiving the SIP messages.

RFC 3261 Section 26.3.1 says only that proxy servers, redirect servers and registrars should possess a site certificate whose subject corresponds to their canonical hostname. Because the RFC gives no guideline on exactly where to put identities, whether in the subjectAltName field or as a Common Name in the Subject field, the practice of the time was to store the identity in the CN field of the certificate instead of the subjectAltName extension.

The lack of further guidelines led to ambiguities. There was no guidance on how to interpret the identities, on which identity to choose if more than one identity is present in the certificate, or on the behaviour when multiple identities with different schemes were present. This document shows how the certificates are to be used for mutual authentication when both client and server hold appropriate certificates, gives normative behaviour for matching the DNS query string with an identity stored in the certificate, and specifies matching rules that cover the various subject identity representation options.
sections.plainLanguage: The old SIP rules only talked about a server's own host name, and left open whether a domain name should go in the certificate's Common Name field or in its subjectAltName list. Implementers chose differently, so a client could not tell which name to check. This RFC settles that.

sections.title: Resolving a SIP Domain to a Host
sections.content:
Routing in SIP is performed by having the client execute the procedures of RFC 3263 on a URI called the Application Unique String. Those procedures take a SIP URI as input, extract the domain portion of that URI as a lookup key, and query the Domain Name System to obtain an ordered set of one or more IP addresses with a port number and transport for each address. If the transport indicates the use of TLS, a TLS connection is opened to the server on a specific IP address and port. The server presents an X.509 certificate to the client for verification as part of the initial TLS handshake.

The client extracts identifiers from the Subject and any subjectAltName extension in the certificate, and compares these values to the domain part extracted from the original SIP URI. If any identifier matches, the server is considered authenticated and subsequent signalling can proceed over the TLS connection.

As the RFC's example shows, a request routed to the SIP address sips:alice@example.com requires a secure connection to the SIP domain example.com, because the sips scheme mandates a secure connection. Through DNS the domain name is mapped to a set of host addresses and transports, and the entity creating the connection selects an address suitable for TLS. When the connection is established, the server presents a certificate asserting the identity sip:example.com. Because the domain part of the SIP URI matches the subject of the certificate, the server is authenticated.

Session Initiation Protocol Secure borrows this pattern of server certificate matching from HTTPS. However, RFC 2818 prefers that the identity be conveyed as a subjectAltName extension of type dNSName rather than the common practice of conveying it in the CN field of the Subject field. This document recommends that the SIP domain identity be conveyed as a subjectAltName extension of type uniformResourceIdentifier.

A domain name in an X.509 certificate is properly interpreted only as a sequence of octets to be compared to the URI used to reach the host. No inference can be made based on the DNS name hierarchy. A valid certificate for example.com does not imply that the owner of that certificate has any relationship at all to subname.example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: The client looks up the domain in DNS, opens a TLS connection to one of the addresses it gets back, and the server shows a certificate. The client then compares the domain it asked for with the names in that certificate. If they match exactly, the server is trusted for that domain.

sections.title: Why Mutual Authentication Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC's example is a SIP trapezoid. A user, alice@example.com, invites bob@example.net for a multimedia session. Alice's outbound proxy, Proxy-A.example.com, uses the normal RFC 3263 resolution rules to find a proxy, Proxy-B.example.net, in the example.net domain that uses TLS. Proxy-A actively establishes an interdomain TLS connection with Proxy-B and each presents a certificate to authenticate that connection.

RFC 3261 Section 26.3.2.2 states that each side of the connection should verify and inspect the certificate of the other, noting the domain name that appears in the certificate for comparison with the header fields of SIP messages. It is, however, silent on whether to use the subjectAltName or the CN of the certificate to obtain the domain name, and on which takes precedence when there are multiple names identifying the holder of the certificate.

The authentication problem for Proxy-A is straightforward. In the certificate it receives from Proxy-B, Proxy-A looks for an identity that is a SIP URI, such as sip:example.net, or a DNS name, example.net, that asserts Proxy-B's authority over the example.net domain.

The problem for Proxy-B is slightly more complex, because it accepts the TLS request passively and so does not hold an equivalent Application Unique String it can use as an anchor when matching identities from Proxy-A's certificate. RFC 3261 Section 26.3.2.2 only tells Proxy-B to compare the domain asserted by the certificate with the domainname portion of the From header field in the INVITE request, and the difficulty is that the domainname in the From header field is not always that of the domain from which the request was received.
sections.plainLanguage: The client side has something to check the certificate against: the domain it was trying to reach. The server side does not, because it accepted the connection without asking for anything in particular. So the server has to use its own policy, such as a list of domains it is willing to peer with.

sections.title: Assigning Certificates in a SIP Domain
sections.content:
It is possible for service providers to continue the practice of using existing certificates for SIP usage with the identity conveyed only in the Subject field, but the RFC gives two reasons to move the identity into the subjectAltName extension field. The extension can hold multiple values, so the same certificate can identify multiple servers or SIP domains. And there is no fixed syntax for the Subject field, so issuers vary in how its content is set, which forces a recipient to use heuristics to extract the identity and again increases opportunities for misinterpretation. Because of these advantages, service providers are strongly encouraged to obtain certificates that contain the identity or identities in the subjectAltName extension field.

When assigning certificates to authoritative servers, a SIP service provider must ensure that the SIP domain used to reach the server appears as an identity in the subjectAltName field, or, for compatibility with existing certificates, in the Subject field of the certificate. In practice this means the provider distributes to its users SIP URIs whose domain portion corresponds to an identity for which the provider has been issued a certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider should get one certificate that names every domain it is authoritative for, and put those names in the extension list rather than in the free-form Subject field. The domain a user dials must then be one the provider holds a certificate for.

sections.title: Finding and Comparing SIP Identities
sections.content:
Implementations, both clients and servers, must determine the validity of a certificate by following the procedures of RFC 5280. They must also check for restrictions on certificate usage declared by any extendedKeyUsage extension, as specified in Section 4.2.1.12 of RFC 5280. The SIP Extended Key Usage document, RFC 5924, defines an extendedKeyUsage for SIP.

Given a certificate that those checks have found acceptable, the RFC sets out how to work out which SIP domain identities it contains. A single certificate can serve more than one purpose, so it might contain identities not acceptable as SIP domain identities and one or more identities that are acceptable.

First, examine each value in the subjectAltName field. The field may be absent, or hold one or more values, and each value has a type. The only types acceptable for encoding a SIP domain identity are URI and DNS. For a URI value, if the scheme is not sip the implementation must not accept the value as a SIP domain identity. If the scheme is sip and the URI contains a userpart, that is an '@' sign, the implementation must not accept the value either, because a value with a userpart identifies an individual user rather than a domain. If the scheme is sip and there is no userinfo component, the implementation must accept the host part as a SIP domain identity. URI scheme tokens are always case insensitive.

For a DNS value, an implementation must accept a domain name system identifier as a SIP domain identity if and only if no other identity matching the sip URI type was found.

Second, if and only if the subjectAltName does not appear in the certificate, the implementation may examine the CN field. If a valid DNS name is found there, the implementation may accept this value as a SIP domain identity. Accepting a DNS name in the CN value is allowed for backward compatibility, but when constructing new certificates the advantages of the subjectAltName extension should be considered.

The procedure yields a set containing zero or more identities. A client uses these identities to authenticate a server and a server uses them to authenticate a client. When comparing two values as SIP domain identities, implementations must compare only the DNS name component of each identifier, and must not use any scheme or parameters in the comparison. The values are compared as DNS names, so the comparison is case insensitive as specified in RFC 4343, and implementations must handle Internationalized Domain Names in accordance with Section 7.2 of RFC 5280.

The values must be matched in their entirety. Implementations must not match suffixes, so foo.example.com does not match example.com. Implementations must not match any form of wildcard, such as a leading . or *., with any other DNS label or sequence of labels. *.example.com matches only *.example.com and not foo.example.com, and .example.com matches only .example.com. RFC 2818 allows the dNSName component to contain a wildcard, and RFC 5280 leaves the interpretation of wildcards to the individual specification, but RFC 3261 gives no guidelines on wildcards, so the rule above prohibits them in certificates for SIP domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first checks the certificate is valid and has the right extended key usage, then collects the names that could stand for a SIP domain. A sip URI without a user name is a domain. A DNS name counts only if there is no sip URI to use. Names are compared whole, ignoring case and ignoring the scheme, and wildcards are not allowed at all.

sections.title: What Each SIP Role Does
sections.content:
Client. A client uses the domain portion of the SIP Application Unique String to query a possibly untrusted DNS to obtain a result set of one or more SRV and A records identifying the server for the domain. The SIP server, when establishing a TLS connection, presents its certificate. The client must determine the SIP domain identities in the server certificate using the procedure in Section 7.1, then must compare the original domain portion of the SIP Application Unique String used as input to the RFC 3263 server location procedures against the SIP domain identities obtained from the certificate. If no identities were found in the server certificate, the server is not authenticated. If the domain extracted from the Application Unique String matches any SIP domain identity from the certificate when compared as described in Section 7.2, the server is authenticated for the domain. If the server is not authenticated, the client must close the connection immediately.

Server. When a server accepts a TLS connection it presents its own X.509 certificate to the client. Servers that wish to authenticate the client will ask the client for a certificate. If the client does not present a certificate, the client must not be considered authenticated. Whether or not to close the connection in that case is a matter of local policy and depends on the server's authentication needs for the connection. Some deployed servers use Digest authentication to authenticate individual requests on the connection and treat the connection as authenticated by those requests for some purposes.

When authenticating the client, the server must obtain the set of SIP domain identities from the client certificate as described in Section 7.1. Because the server accepted the TLS connection passively, unlike a client it does not hold an Application Unique String for comparison, but server policies can use the identity set gathered from the certificate to make authorization decisions. A very open policy would be to accept any X.509 certificate validated by the RFC 5280 procedures and simply log the identity set. A stricter server keeps a list of the SIP domains it accepts connections from and searches the client certificate's identities in that list. The decision of whether an authenticated connection is appropriate for routing new requests to the client domain is independent of whether the connection is authenticated, and the connect-reuse document discusses that aspect.

Proxy. A proxy must use the procedures defined for a User Agent Server when authenticating a connection from a client, and the procedures defined for a User Agent Client when requesting an authenticated connection to a User Agent Server. If a proxy adds a Record-Route when forwarding a request with the expectation that the route will use secure connections, the proxy must insert into the Record-Route header a URI that corresponds to an identity for which the proxy holds a certificate. If it does not insert such a URI, creating a secure connection using the Record-Route value as the Application Unique String will be impossible.

Registrar and redirect server. A SIP registrar, acting as a server, follows the normative behaviour of Section 7.4. When it accepts a TLS connection from the client it presents its certificate, and depending on registrar policy it can challenge the client with HTTP Digest. A SIP redirect server follows the normative behaviour of a User Agent Server.

Virtual servers. Where multiple domains are managed by a single application, a certificate can contain multiple subjects by having distinct identities in the subjectAltName field, as specified in RFC 4474. Clients seeking to authenticate a server on such a virtual host can still follow Section 7.3 to find the identity matching the Application Unique String used to query DNS. Alternatively, if the TLS client hello server_name extension from RFC 4366 is supported, the client should use that extension to request a certificate corresponding to the specific domain it is seeking to reach.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks the server's certificate against the domain it wanted and drops the connection if they do not match. The server checks the client's certificate against its own list of acceptable peer domains. A proxy that tells downstream servers to come back to it over TLS has to give an address that appears in its own certificate.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goals of TLS, when used with X.509 certificates, include confidentiality, meaning that packets tunnelled through TLS can be read only by the sender and the receiver; integrity, meaning that those packets cannot be undetectably modified on the connection; and authentication, meaning that each principal is authenticated to the other as possessing a private key for which a certificate has been issued, that the certificate has not been revoked, and that it is verifiable by a certificate chain leading to a locally configured trust anchor.

The RFC expects appropriate processing of domain certificates to add the following guarantees at the application level. Confidentiality: SIPS messages from alice@example.com to bob@example.net can be read only by alice@example.com, bob@example.net, and the SIP proxies issued with domain certificates for example.com or example.net. Integrity: those messages cannot be undetectably modified on the links between those parties. Authentication: alice@example.com and proxy.example.com are mutually authenticated, and proxy.example.com is authenticated to alice@example.com as an authoritative proxy for domain example.com, with similar mutual authentication between proxy.example.com and proxy.example.net and between proxy.example.net and bob@example.net, so that alice@example.com is transitively mutually authenticated to bob@example.net.

Digest on a connection. Digest authentication in SIP authenticates the message sender to the challenging User Agent Server. As commonly deployed it gives only very limited integrity protection of the authenticated message, and it has no provision for binding the authentication to any attribute of the transport. Many existing SIP deployments have used the Digest authentication of one or more messages on a particular transport connection as a way to authenticate the connection itself, by implication authenticating other, unauthenticated messages on that connection, and some have even authenticated a UDP source address and port in the same way. That use goes beyond what the Digest mechanism was designed to provide. A SIP implementation should not use the Digest authentication of one message on a TCP connection, or from a UDP peer, to infer any authentication of other messages on that connection or from that peer. Authentication of the domain at the other end of a connection should be accomplished with TLS and the certificate validation rules of this specification instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Two domains can therefore be sure of each other's identity through the proxies in between. The RFC also warns against a shortcut: proving one message with Digest does not prove the connection, and the domain check should be done with the TLS certificate instead.

viz.caption: Which names in a certificate count as a SIP domain identity

items.title: URI with another scheme
items.text: Must not be accepted as a SIP domain identity.

items.title: sip URI with a userpart
items.text: Must not be accepted: it identifies an individual user, not a domain.

items.title: sip URI without userinfo
items.text: The host part must be accepted as a SIP domain identity.

items.title: DNS name in subjectAltName
items.text: Accepted if and only if no other identity matching the sip URI type was found.

items.title: DNS name in the CN field
items.text: May be accepted, and only when subjectAltName is absent from the certificate.
